subject: Orthopaedics
q: Image described: wrist X-ray showing metaphyseal cupping and fraying with a rachitic picture; renal ultrasound showing bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. A 4-year-old with bowed legs and failure to thrive shows hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine pH. Which condition best explains this picture?
why: XLH causes rickets with low phosphate but normal acid-base status, no nephrocalcinosis as a primary feature
Nutritional rickets does not typically cause hyperchloremic acidosis or nephrocalcinosis
Correct
Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia and brown tumours, not a rachitic/acidotic picture in a young child.
exp: Distal RTA causes an inability to acidify urine (persistently alkaline urine pH despite systemic metabolic acidosis), leading to nephrocalcinosis and a rachitic bone picture from chronic acidosis and its effects on calcium/vitamin D handling — nephrocalcinosis plus rickets plus hyperchloremic normal-anion-gap acidosis points to a tubular acidification defect rather than nutritional or phosphate-wasting rickets.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 3-year-old girl presents with painless swelling of the right knee for 8 weeks, morning stiffness lasting 45 minutes, and no fever. ANA is positive; inflammatory markers are mildly raised. Beyond joint-directed therapy, what is the most important next step in her management?
opts: Bone marrow biopsy to exclude leukaemia
Blood culture and joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis
X-ray of the hip to exclude Perthes disease
Referral for slit-lamp ophthalmological screening for asymptomatic uveitis
why: The chronic, afebrile, joint-limited course makes leukaemia unlikely as the leading concern
Septic arthritis is acute, febrile, and toxic-looking, not this chronic painless course
Perthes presents with limp/hip-referred pain typically in boys, not this ANA-positive picture
Correct — the single most important disease-specific screening step.
exp: This is the classic picture of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) — young girl, few joints, ANA-positive, chronic painless swelling — the subgroup carrying the highest risk of asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis, which can silently cause blindness unless screened by regular slit-lamp examination regardless of eye symptoms.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Image described: photograph of the posterior shoulder showing visible wasting/hollowing over the infraspinatus fossa compared to the normal side. A competitive volleyball player has vague posterior shoulder pain and weakness of external rotation, with preserved deltoid and supraspinatus-mediated abduction strength. Which nerve is most likely involved?
opts: Suprascapular nerve (entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch)
why: Correct
Axillary nerve injury weakens deltoid (preserved here) with regimental-badge sensory loss
Long thoracic nerve injury causes scapular winging, not infraspinatus wasting
Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion with lateral forearm sensory loss, unrelated here.
exp: Suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch (often from a paralabral cyst or repetitive overhead/serving action) selectively weakens and wastes the infraspinatus while sparing supraspinatus and deltoid if the lesion is distal to the supraspinatus branch — a useful localizing pattern versus a more proximal suprascapular-notch lesion affecting both muscles.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Image described: lateral wrist X-ray showing the distal radial fragment displaced volarly (garden-spade deformity). An elderly woman fell onto the dorsum of her flexed, outstretched wrist. Which fracture does this represent?
why: Colles results from a fall on an extended wrist with dorsal displacement — the opposite mechanism and deformity
Correct
Barton fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation involving the articular rim, a distinct pattern
Galeazzi involves a distal radial shaft fracture with DRUJ disruption, not this deformity.
exp: A Smith fracture (reverse Colles) results from a fall on the flexed wrist/dorsum of the hand, displacing the distal radial fragment volarly, producing the "garden-spade" deformity — the mirror image of the Colles fracture's dorsally-displaced "dinner-fork" deformity from a fall on an extended, outstretched hand.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 68-year-old man with known cervical spondylosis falls forward and strikes his chin, sustaining a hyperextension neck injury. He develops weakness disproportionately greater in the upper limbs than the lower limbs, with preserved perianal sensation. Which spinal cord injury pattern best explains this?
why: Anterior cord syndrome follows flexion injury/anterior spinal artery compromise, with bilateral motor and pain/temperature loss but preserved proprioception — not this pattern
Brown-Sequard follows hemisection, causing ipsilateral motor/proprioceptive loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss, not symmetric arm-greater-than-leg weakness
Correct
Posterior cord syndrome (rare) causes proprioceptive/vibration loss, not this motor pattern.
exp: Central cord syndrome classically follows a hyperextension injury in an older patient with pre-existing cervical spondylosis/canal stenosis; the centrally-located cervical tracts serving the upper limbs are disproportionately affected compared to the more peripherally-located lower-limb tracts, producing arm-greater-than-leg weakness, often with sacral sparing — the most common incomplete cord injury syndrome overall.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A child has dense but brittle long bones with pathological fractures and pancytopenia from marrow encroachment, with an Erlenmeyer-flask widening at the distal femoral metaphysis on X-ray. Which condition is this?
why: Correct - osteoclast failure to resorb bone is the defect
OI causes fragile thin bones, not dense ones
Rickets shows metaphyseal cupping/fraying with undermineralized bone, not density
Fibrous dysplasia shows ground-glass lesions, not this systemic pancytopenic picture
exp: Osteopetrosis (Albers-Schonberg disease) results from osteoclast failure to resorb bone (carbonic anhydrase II or TCIRG1 mutations), producing dense but brittle bone-within-bone and marble-bone appearance with erlenmeyer flask deformity; marrow encroachment causes pancytopenia and extramedullary hematopoiesis.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Progressive bowing of the leg below the knee in an obese toddler, with an increased medial proximal tibial metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle on X-ray, is characteristic of which condition?
why: Physiological bowing is symmetric, resolves by 2 years, with a normal angle
Correct
Rickets shows metaphyseal cupping/fraying with biochemical abnormalities, not an isolated angle finding
OI presents with fractures and blue sclerae, not isolated tibial bowing
exp: Blount's disease is a growth disorder of the medial proximal tibial physis causing progressive, often asymmetric bowing beyond 2-3 years of age; an increased metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle (Drennan's angle) distinguishes pathological Blount's from physiological bowing, which resolves spontaneously by age 2.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Weakness of elbow flexion and forearm supination with sensory loss over the lateral forearm following penetrating axillary trauma points to injury of which nerve?
why: Correct
Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness and regimental-badge sensory loss over the lateral shoulder, not forearm
Median nerve injury causes weak pronation/wrist flexion and thenar sensory loss
Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop, not elbow flexion weakness
exp: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7) innervates biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis (elbow flexion/supination) and continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm; it can be injured in the coracobrachialis segment during axillary trauma.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A fracture of the distal one-third radial shaft with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint is termed which injury?
why: Monteggia involves a proximal ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation, not a distal radial fracture
Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation, without named DRUJ disruption
Smith fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar angulation
Correct
exp: Galeazzi fracture-dislocation is a distal radial shaft fracture with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ); it usually needs ORIF of the radius plus DRUJ stabilization, distinguishing it from a Monteggia injury's proximal ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A hyperextension cervical spine injury producing bilateral fracture through the pars interarticularis of C2, with traumatic anterolisthesis of C2 on C3, is known as which fracture?
why: Jefferson fracture is a C1 ring burst fracture from axial loading
Correct
Clay-shoveler's fracture is a spinous process avulsion from sudden flexion
Chance fracture is a thoracolumbar flexion-distraction injury, classically from a lap belt
exp: Hangman's fracture is a traumatic bilateral pars interarticularis fracture of C2 from hyperextension-distraction, producing anterolisthesis of C2 on C3; it can be relatively stable given the wide canal diameter at this level but always needs cord-compromise assessment.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: The most common benign tumor of bone, a painless juxta-metaphyseal bony projection with a cartilage cap continuous with the underlying medullary cavity, is which lesion?
why: Correct
Enchondroma is an intramedullary lesion, commonly in hand phalanges, not a surface outgrowth
Osteoid osteoma is small and painful with NSAID-relieved night pain and a lucent nidus
GCT is an epiphyseal, eccentric, soap-bubble lesion in skeletally mature patients
exp: Osteochondroma (exostosis) is the most common benign bone tumor, arising from aberrant physeal cartilage forming a cartilage-capped outgrowth continuous with the parent bone's cortex and medulla; malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is suggested by a cartilage cap over 2 cm or growth after skeletal maturity.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Image described: ankle radiograph (AP and lateral views) showing a fracture of the distal fibula at the level of the tibiofibular syndesmosis, with widening of the mortise. According to the Weber classification, a fibular fracture at this level is classified as:
why: Correct - a fracture at the syndesmosis level is Weber B.
Wrong - Weber A is infrasyndesmotic, below the syndesmosis.
Wrong - Weber C is suprasyndesmotic, above the syndesmosis.
Wrong - not a recognised Weber category.
exp: The Weber (AO) classification of lateral malleolar fractures is based on fracture level relative to the tibiofibular syndesmosis: A below (usually stable), B at the level (variable stability), C above (unstable, syndesmosis disrupted) - a widened mortise on X-ray, regardless of Weber type, signals instability requiring surgical fixation.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 55-year-old man presents with a slowly progressive dull ache in the pelvis. Imaging shows a lytic lesion with popcorn-like/ring-and-arc calcification arising in the pelvic bone, with cortical destruction. Histopathology shows malignant chondrocytes producing cartilaginous matrix. The diagnosis is:
why: Wrong - osteosarcoma classically shows sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle in a younger, metaphyseal patient.
Wrong - Ewing sarcoma shows onion-skin periosteal reaction in a younger patient with small round blue cells.
Correct - matches the older age, pelvic location, and popcorn calcification.
Wrong - osteochondroma is a benign exostosis with a cartilage cap, not a destructive lytic malignant lesion.
exp: Chondrosarcoma is the second most common primary malignant bone tumour after osteosarcoma, typically affecting older adults, arising centrally in the axial skeleton (pelvis, ribs) or proximal long bones; the popcorn/ring-and-arc calcification pattern reflects cartilaginous matrix and, combined with cortical destruction, distinguishes it from a benign cartilage tumour.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 10-month-old infant fed exclusively on boiled cow's milk (no fruits or vegetables introduced) presents with irritability, pseudoparalysis of the legs, and swollen, tender lower limbs. Radiograph shows a dense white line at the metaphysis with a lucent zone beneath it, a thin ground-glass cortical shell, and subperiosteal new bone formation. The most likely diagnosis is:
why: Wrong - rickets shows metaphyseal cupping/fraying and widened growth plates, not subperiosteal haemorrhage.
Wrong - OI shows multiple fractures with normal metaphyses and blue sclerae.
Correct - matches the diet history and classic radiographic constellation of scurvy.
Wrong - must always be considered, but the findings described are classic for scurvy, not abuse.
exp: Infantile scurvy (Barlow's disease) results from prolonged Vitamin C deficiency, classically in infants given only boiled cow's milk without fruit/vegetable supplementation; defective collagen synthesis causes subperiosteal haemorrhage producing pseudoparalysis and tenderness, with characteristic radiographic signs - Frankel's white line, Trummerfeld zone, and corner/ring sign - reversing rapidly with vitamin C replacement.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Image described: lateral wrist radiograph showing a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation and dorsal displacement of the distal fragment, radial shortening, and an associated ulnar styloid fracture, producing a dinner-fork deformity clinically. This injury typically results from which mechanism?
opts: Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH) with wrist extended
Direct blow to the dorsum of the wrist
why: Correct - classic FOOSH mechanism with wrist extended.
Wrong - a fall on a flexed wrist produces the opposite pattern, Smith's fracture with volar displacement.
Wrong - direct blow is not the classic mechanism for this fracture pattern.
Wrong - twisting injury is more typical of forearm shaft fractures.
exp: Colles' fracture is the most common wrist fracture, classically in elderly women with osteoporosis after a fall onto an outstretched, dorsiflexed hand, producing the dinner-fork deformity from dorsal displacement/angulation of the distal fragment plus radial shortening; the mirror-image volarly-displaced injury is Smith's fracture.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A woman undergoes axillary lymph node dissection as part of breast cancer surgery. Post-operatively, the medial border of her scapula protrudes prominently backward when she pushes against a wall with outstretched arms. The nerve most likely injured, and the muscle it supplies, are:
why: Wrong - spinal accessory nerve injury causes trapezius palsy with a different winging pattern, more linked to posterior neck triangle surgery.
Wrong - axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness and regimental-badge sensory loss, not scapular winging.
Wrong - thoracodorsal nerve injury weakens latissimus dorsi, not scapular winging.
Correct - classic medial winging from serratus anterior paralysis.
exp: The long thoracic nerve's superficial course on the surface of serratus anterior makes it vulnerable during axillary node dissection, mastectomy, and even prolonged shoulder-strap pressure; serratus anterior normally holds the scapula against the chest wall, so its paralysis produces classic medial winging, accentuated on forward pushing against resistance - usually managed conservatively as most cases recover spontaneously over months.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A new mother who frequently lifts her infant with her thumb extended complains of pain over the radial aspect of the wrist, worsened by making a fist around the thumb and deviating the wrist toward the little finger. This specific provocative test is called:
why: Wrong - Phalen's test is used for carpal tunnel syndrome.
Wrong - Tinel's test involves tapping over a nerve, not specific to this condition.
Correct - the classic provocative test for De Quervain's tenosynovitis.
Wrong - Watson's test assesses scapholunate ligament instability.
exp: De Quervain's tenosynovitis is stenosing tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment, abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons, at the radial styloid, common in new mothers from repetitive thumb-in-extension lifting of an infant; Finkelstein's test, thumb flexed into palm with the wrist ulnar-deviated, reproduces sharp radial wrist pain and is diagnostic.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A congenital metabolic bone disorder due to deficient tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase activity, causing defective bone and tooth mineralization with paradoxically LOW serum alkaline phosphatase, is known as which condition?
why: Osteopetrosis is an osteoclast dysfunction causing dense brittle bones, without characteristically low alkaline phosphatase
Fibrous dysplasia is a localized fibro-osseous lesion unrelated to alkaline phosphatase levels
Correct - hypophosphatasia causes rachitic features with a characteristically low serum alkaline phosphatase
Osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen type 1 disorder causing bone fragility, not an alkaline phosphatase deficiency disease
exp: Hypophosphatasia is the one metabolic bone disease where serum alkaline phosphatase is low rather than high - nearly every other cause of rickets or osteomalacia shows elevated alkaline phosphatase from active bone turnover, making a low level in a child with rachitic features a red flag for this diagnosis.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: As per the Ponseti method for congenital talipes equinovarus, serial manipulation and casting should ideally begin at which age for the best correction outcomes?
opts: After the child begins walking, around 12-15 months
Between 6 months and 1 year of age
At 3-6 months of age, once systemically stable
As early as possible in the neonatal period, ideally within the first 1-2 weeks of life
why: Far too late, ligamentous laxity needed for correction is largely lost by walking age
Still delayed compared to the recommended window
Later than ideal, though still used if presentation is delayed
Correct - neonatal ligaments and cartilage are maximally pliable, giving the best correction
exp: Earlier initiation of Ponseti casting within the first couple of weeks of life gives the best correction because neonatal collagen and ligaments are maximally pliable - delayed presentation still responds to Ponseti casting but typically needs more casts and carries a higher chance of needing adjunctive tenotomy or later relapse.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A newborn delivered by breech extraction with forceful traction on an abducted, hyperextended arm develops a clawed hand with loss of finger flexion and intrinsic muscle function, but preserved shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis are also noted. Which brachial plexus injury does this represent?
opts: Total or pan brachial plexus palsy
Klumpke's palsy, lower trunk C8-T1, with Horner syndrome
why: Erb's palsy causes the opposite pattern, a waiter's tip posture with hand function preserved
Radial nerve palsy causes wrist drop and is not a birth brachial plexus injury pattern
Total plexus palsy would show a flail, insensate arm involving all segments, not isolated distal involvement
Correct - lower trunk involvement causes a claw hand with preserved proximal function, and T1 sympathetic chain damage causes Horner syndrome
exp: Klumpke's palsy, though rarer than Erb's palsy, is recognized by the claw-hand pattern with intact proximal shoulder and elbow movement but paralyzed intrinsic hand and finger flexor muscles, plus Horner syndrome when the T1 sympathetic outflow is involved - always examine the pupil and eyelid in a newborn with a lower brachial plexus pattern.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 22-year-old man falls onto an outstretched hand and presents with wrist pain and point tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Initial wrist X-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate next step, given the specific risk here?
opts: Reassure and discharge since the X-ray is normal
Immobilize in a thumb spica splint or cast and repeat imaging in 10-14 days
Proceed directly to open reduction and internal fixation
Apply a below-elbow cast for a distal radius fracture
why: Discharging without immobilization risks missing an occult scaphoid fracture that can progress to avascular necrosis if untreated
Correct - snuffbox tenderness with a normal initial X-ray is managed as a presumed scaphoid fracture with immobilization and repeat imaging or MRI
Surgery is not indicated without a confirmed displaced fracture
Tenderness localizes to the scaphoid region, not the distal radius, so this does not match a distal radius fracture
exp: Scaphoid fractures are notoriously easy to miss on initial X-ray because the fracture line may not be visible for 1-2 weeks, and because the scaphoid's retrograde blood supply risks avascular necrosis and nonunion if untreated, snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand is treated as a fracture until proven otherwise.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 45-year-old recreational badminton player felt a sudden pop at the back of the ankle while lunging, with immediate difficulty bearing weight and a palpable gap above the heel. Squeezing the calf with the patient prone and knee flexed produces no plantarflexion of the foot. Which injury and clinical test does this describe?
opts: Peroneal tendon subluxation, positive peroneal compression test
Posterior tibialis tendon rupture, positive too-many-toes sign
Achilles tendon rupture, positive Thompson or Simmonds test
Ankle sprain of the lateral ligament complex, positive anterior drawer test
why: Peroneal tendon subluxation presents with lateral ankle snapping and pain, not a heel gap or absent plantarflexion
Posterior tibialis rupture causes acquired flatfoot with the too-many-toes sign, not an acute pop with a heel gap
Correct - the sudden pop, palpable gap above the heel, and absent plantarflexion on calf squeeze confirm Achilles tendon rupture
An ankle sprain would show lateral ligament tenderness and a positive anterior drawer test, not an absent Thompson response
exp: The Thompson or Simmonds test, squeezing the calf with the patient prone and knees flexed while watching for foot plantarflexion, is the key bedside test for Achilles tendon integrity - its absence with a sudden pop, palpable tendon gap, and weak plantarflexion confirms a complete rupture, most often in middle-aged weekend-warrior athletes doing push-off sports.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 62-year-old retired mill worker develops several weeks of worsening back pain, fatigue, and recurrent infections. Skull X-ray shows multiple well-defined punched-out lytic lesions without a sclerotic rim. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals a monoclonal M band. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
why: Prostate cancer metastases are classically osteoblastic and sclerotic, not lytic, and would not produce an M band
Osteosarcoma occurs in a younger age group at long-bone metaphyses with a sunburst periosteal reaction, not multifocal skull lesions with an M band
Giant cell tumor is a solitary epiphyseal lesion in young adults, not a multifocal skull disease with paraproteinemia
Correct - multiple myeloma classically shows punched-out lytic lesions without sclerosis plus a monoclonal gammopathy
exp: Multiple myeloma's punched-out lytic skull lesions lack a sclerotic rim because myeloma cells activate osteoclasts via RANKL without a compensatory osteoblastic response, the opposite radiographic pattern to prostate cancer's typically osteoblastic bone metastases, a classic pairing tested to differentiate lytic versus blastic bone disease.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 9-year-old boy falls onto an outstretched, pronated forearm and presents with a deformed proximal forearm; radiographs show a fracture of the proximal third of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head. Which nerve is most likely injured, producing finger and thumb drop with preserved wrist extension?
why: Correct — PIN winds around the radial neck through the arcade of Frohse, vulnerable to radial head dislocation
Ulnar nerve is at risk in medial elbow injuries/supracondylar fractures, not Monteggia
Median nerve injury occurs with supracondylar fractures or elbow dislocation, not typically Monteggia
AIN is a pure motor branch causing weak pinch (OK sign) in supracondylar fractures, not Monteggia
exp: Monteggia fracture-dislocation (proximal ulna fracture + radial head dislocation) is classically associated with posterior interosseous nerve injury, producing finger/thumb drop with preserved wrist extension because ECRL is spared — distinguishing it from a complete radial nerve palsy.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 28-year-old man involved in a head-on road traffic accident presents with the right hip flexed, adducted, and internally rotated, and is unable to dorsiflex the ipsilateral foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why: Femoral nerve injury causes quadriceps weakness/loss of knee extension, not seen here
Correct — the sciatic nerve, particularly its peroneal division, is stretched by posterior femoral head displacement
Obturator nerve injury causes hip adductor weakness, not implicated in posterior dislocation
Superior gluteal nerve injury causes Trendelenburg gait, unrelated to this mechanism
exp: Posterior hip dislocation (dashboard injury) drives the femoral head posteriorly, stretching or compressing the sciatic nerve against the posterior acetabular wall and producing foot drop; it is a surgical emergency needing reduction within 6 hours to reduce avascular necrosis risk.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 16-year-old boy has dull aching pain in the left tibial shaft for several months, characteristically worse at night and dramatically relieved within minutes of aspirin or ibuprofen. Imaging shows a small round lucent nidus with surrounding dense sclerosis. What is the diagnosis?
why: Osteosarcoma shows a sunburst appearance with Codman triangle and lacks this dramatic NSAID relief
Ewing sarcoma shows onion-skin periosteal reaction, a diaphyseal round-cell tumour without a nidus
Correct — a nidus with florid NSAID-responsive night pain is pathognomonic of osteoid osteoma
Osteochondroma is a painless bony outgrowth with a cartilage cap, not painful at night
exp: Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone-forming tumour of adolescents causing night pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs (tumour-derived prostaglandin production) with a small radiolucent nidus and surrounding sclerosis; CT localizes the nidus and radiofrequency ablation is now first-line treatment.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 35-year-old man from a high-TB-burden area presents with weeks of low-grade fever, night sweats, and worsening mid-back pain, with a visible angular kyphotic deformity (gibbus) and a soft fluctuant paravertebral swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Pyogenic osteomyelitis is more acute with marked local inflammation, and rarely causes a cold abscess
Ankylosing spondylitis causes progressive stiffness in a young HLA-B27-positive patient, not fever/abscess
Metastatic collapse usually spares the disc space and lacks fever/abscess
Correct — a cold abscess and gibbus with subacute fever is classic for Pott's disease
exp: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) affects the anterior vertebral body across the disc space, producing progressive gibbus deformity and a paravertebral cold abscess that tracks along fascial planes without marked warmth/erythema; MRI is the imaging of choice and ATT is the mainstay of treatment.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 13-year-old footballer reports gradually worsening anterior knee pain for two months, worse with running and jumping, with localized tenderness and a bony prominence over the tibial tuberosity, and an otherwise normal knee joint examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — a tender tibial tuberosity prominence in an adolescent athlete is classic Osgood-Schlatter disease
Patellar dislocation presents with acute instability episodes and haemarthrosis, not gradual apophyseal pain
Osteochondritis dissecans causes intra-articular pain/locking from an osteochondral fragment, not isolated tuberosity tenderness
Septic arthritis presents acutely with fever, effusion, and severe restriction of movement, not a two-month indolent course
exp: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity from repetitive quadriceps pull through the patellar tendon in adolescent athletes; it is a clinical diagnosis managed conservatively (activity modification, ice, quadriceps stretching) and is self-limiting once the apophysis fuses.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A female infant born by breech presentation at term is being evaluated for developmental dysplasia of the hip. Which factor is the strongest risk factor warranting screening hip ultrasound at 6 weeks of age?
why: DDH is far more common in females, roughly 4-6:1, not males
Correct - breech presentation is the single strongest DDH risk factor
Twin gestation is a weaker, less consistent risk factor than breech
Prematurity is not a major established DDH risk factor, unlike breech, female sex, and family history
exp: Breech presentation is the single strongest risk factor for DDH, followed by female sex and positive family history; screening hip ultrasound at 6 weeks is recommended for infants with any of these risk factors, since clinical tests lose sensitivity beyond the neonatal period.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 65-year-old man with known prostate carcinoma presents with severe low back pain. X-ray shows multiple sclerotic lesions in the lumbar vertebrae. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Osteoblastic bone metastasis from prostate carcinoma
why: Multiple myeloma produces punched-out lytic lesions, not sclerotic ones.
Paget disease shows a mosaic bone pattern with cortical thickening, unrelated to a malignancy history.
Correct - prostate carcinoma classically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) skeletal metastases in the axial skeleton.
Senile osteoporosis causes diffuse bone lucency, not focal sclerotic lesions.
exp: Prostate carcinoma classically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) skeletal metastases, mostly in the spine and pelvis, unlike breast, lung, kidney, or thyroid cancer which typically cause osteolytic lesions; markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium supports the diagnosis.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 40-year-old farmer from an endemic fluoride-belt region presents with chronic back stiffness, restricted spinal mobility, and radiographs showing increased bone density with ligamentous calcification of the spine. Which condition is most likely?
why: Ankylosing spondylitis is HLA-B27-associated, typically in younger patients with sacroiliitis, without endemic-water association.
Paget disease shows a mosaic lytic-sclerotic pattern with cortical thickening, a distinct radiologic picture.
Osteopetrosis is a genetic osteoclast defect presenting from childhood, not adult-onset endemic disease.
Correct - skeletal fluorosis from chronic excess fluoride intake causes increased bone density and ligamentous calcification in endemic regions.
exp: Skeletal fluorosis, endemic in fluoride-belt regions of India, results from chronic excess fluoride intake causing increased bone density, ligamentous and paraspinal calcification, and progressive spinal stiffness that can mimic ankylosing spondylitis; endemic residence and water fluoride level are the distinguishing clues.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 45-year-old woman with hypothyroidism presents with nocturnal tingling and numbness in the thumb, index, and middle finger with thenar wasting, and a positive Tinel's sign at the wrist. Which nerve is most likely compressed?
why: Ulnar nerve compression causes little/ring finger sensory loss with claw hand, not thumb/index symptoms.
Correct - carpal tunnel syndrome results from median nerve compression at the wrist beneath the flexor retinaculum.
Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop and dorsal hand sensory loss, not this distribution.
Anterior interosseous nerve is a pure motor branch with no sensory symptoms.
exp: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from median nerve compression beneath the flexor retinaculum, causing nocturnal paresthesia in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger with thenar wasting in advanced cases; hypothyroidism, pregnancy, diabetes, and repetitive strain are recognized risk factors.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 28-year-old man following a fibular neck fracture develops inability to dorsiflex and evert the foot, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is injured?
why: Tibial nerve injury causes loss of plantarflexion/inversion, not foot drop
Sural nerve is purely sensory (posterolateral leg)
Saphenous nerve is purely sensory (medial leg/foot)
Correct - common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck and is vulnerable there
exp: The common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck, making it vulnerable to fracture or compression - injury causes foot drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 28-year-old woman with closed distal femoral epiphyses presents with knee pain, and an X-ray shows an eccentric, lytic soap-bubble lesion extending from the metaphysis right up to the subchondral bone of the epiphysis, with no periosteal reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct
Osteosarcoma classically shows sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman's triangle in a skeletally immature patient
Ewing sarcoma shows onion-skin periosteal reaction, diaphyseal, in children/adolescents
Osteochondroma is an exophytic cartilage-capped bony projection, not a lytic lesion
exp: Giant cell tumour of bone occurs in skeletally mature patients (20-40 years) at the epiphysis/metaphysis extending to subchondral bone, appearing as a lytic soap-bubble lesion without periosteal reaction, and carries a small risk of malignant transformation and pulmonary metastasis.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 50-year-old woman with hypercalcemia and markedly elevated parathyroid hormone is found to have a lytic long-bone lesion on X-ray; biopsy shows numerous osteoclast-like giant cells within a fibrovascular stroma. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism (osteitis fibrosa cystica)
why: Giant cell tumor of bone is a distinct primary neoplasm at the epiphysis of a young adult, without hypercalcemia/raised PTH
Aneurysmal bone cyst is a blood-filled cystic lesion unrelated to PTH/calcium
Correct — classic brown tumor in the setting of hyperparathyroidism
Osteosarcoma shows sunburst periosteal reaction in adolescents, not linked to hypercalcemia
exp: Brown tumors (osteitis fibrosa cystica) are a lytic bone manifestation of primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism, histologically showing osteoclast-rich giant cells in a fibrovascular stroma — they mimic giant cell tumor of bone histologically but are distinguished by the biochemical context (raised calcium and PTH) and regress once the hyperparathyroidism is corrected.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A child treated conservatively for a supracondylar humerus fracture develops a claw-hand deformity with fixed finger flexion several weeks later. What is this condition called?
why: Erb's palsy is a birth brachial plexus injury (C5-C6) causing 'waiter's tip' posture, unrelated to fracture ischemia
Cubitus varus is a bony malunion (gunstock deformity), not a soft-tissue ischemic contracture
Correct — follows missed compartment syndrome after supracondylar fracture
Klumpke's palsy is a lower plexus (C8-T1) birth injury, a different mechanism
exp: Volkmann's ischemic contracture follows missed/inadequately treated compartment syndrome after supracondylar fracture — forearm flexor muscle ischemia leads to fibrosis, producing a fixed claw-hand deformity; early recognition of compartment syndrome (pain on passive extension) prevents it.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 2-year-old girl cries and refuses to move her arm after being swung up by the wrist. The elbow is held slightly flexed and pronated, with no swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Supracondylar fracture typically follows a fall with visible swelling/deformity, not traction
Lateral condyle fracture is fall-related with local swelling
Monteggia involves an ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation from direct trauma
Correct — traction mechanism with pronated flexed elbow and no swelling is classic nursemaid's elbow
exp: Radial head subluxation ('pulled elbow') results from axial traction on a pronated, extended arm, slipping the annular ligament over the radial head; it is a clinical diagnosis and reduces with gentle supination-flexion, no imaging usually needed.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 30-year-old man sustains an open tibial shaft fracture with a 3 cm wound, moderate soft-tissue damage, and no significant periosteal stripping or contamination. How is this classified per Gustilo-Anderson?
why: Type I is a wound less than 1 cm with minimal damage, smaller than described
Type IIIA involves extensive soft-tissue damage with adequate bone coverage, more severe
Type IIIB involves bone exposure requiring flap coverage, clearly more severe
Correct — 1-10 cm wound with moderate damage fits Type II
exp: Gustilo-Anderson Type II open fractures have a wound 1-10 cm long with moderate soft-tissue damage but without extensive stripping, flap requirement, or gross contamination — between the minimal Type I and severe Type III subtypes, guiding antibiotic choice and debridement urgency.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 14-year-old boy with chronic kidney disease on dialysis develops bone pain, and labs show elevated PTH, elevated phosphate, and low-normal calcium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency alone
why: Correct - phosphate retention and impaired vitamin D activation drive secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD
Primary hyperparathyroidism arises from an autonomous parathyroid lesion and would show hypercalcemia, not low-normal calcium
Adynamic bone disease also occurs in dialysis patients but shows low/normal PTH with reduced bone turnover, not the elevated PTH seen here
Isolated vitamin D deficiency rickets would not typically show the phosphate retention seen in CKD
exp: Renal osteodystrophy in CKD results from phosphate retention and impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D, both driving secondary hyperparathyroidism - the biochemical triad of elevated PTH, elevated phosphate, and low/low-normal calcium in a CKD patient with bone pain should point here rather than to primary hyperparathyroidism or isolated nutritional rickets.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 5-year-old boy has hip pain, fever of 39 degree C, refusal to bear weight, and an ESR of 45 mm/hr after a recent viral illness. Which clinical prediction rule helps differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis in this child?
why: Ottawa ankle rules guide ankle X-ray decisions, unrelated
Alvarado score is used for appendicitis
Correct - Kocher criteria stratify the probability of septic arthritis in an irritable hip
Ranson's criteria assess pancreatitis severity, unrelated
exp: The Kocher criteria (fever above 38.5 degree C, inability to bear weight, ESR above 40mm/hr, WBC above 12,000/microL) stratify the probability of septic arthritis versus transient synovitis in a child with an acutely irritable hip, guiding the decision for urgent joint aspiration.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 45-year-old woman with chronic malabsorption (post gastric bypass) presents with diffuse bone pain and a waddling gait; X-ray shows pseudofractures (Looser zones) in the pubic rami and femoral neck, with low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The most likely diagnosis is:
why: Correct — adult presentation with Looser zones is osteomalacia
Rickets is the paediatric pre-epiphyseal-fusion form and shows metaphyseal cupping/fraying, not Looser zones

Paget disease can itself show pseudofractures on the convex cortex, but shows normal calcium/phosphate/25(OH)D with markedly raised alkaline phosphatase — the low 25(OH)D and malabsorption history here point to osteomalacia
Osteoporosis shows reduced bone density with normal mineralisation, without Looser zones
exp: Osteomalacia is the adult counterpart of rickets, occurring after epiphyseal fusion, due to defective mineralisation of osteoid from vitamin D or phosphate deficiency; it presents with diffuse bone pain, proximal myopathy causing a waddling gait, and the radiographic hallmark of Looser zones — characteristic transverse pseudofractures perpendicular to the cortex at mechanical stress sites (medial femoral neck, pubic rami, scapula, ribs).

subject: Orthopaedics
q: An infant sustains multiple long-bone fractures with only minimal trauma; examination reveals distinctly blue sclerae, and there is a family history of early-onset hearing loss and easy fracturing. The most likely underlying molecular defect is in:
why: Correct — type I collagen defect underlies osteogenesis imperfecta
Vitamin D receptor defects cause vitamin D-resistant rickets, not this blue-sclera fracture syndrome
FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia, a different skeletal phenotype
ALPL mutations cause hypophosphatasia, presenting with defective mineralisation and low alkaline phosphatase, not this classic triad
exp: Osteogenesis imperfecta is most commonly caused by autosomal dominant COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations affecting type I collagen, producing recurrent low-trauma fractures, blue sclerae (thin sclera revealing underlying uveal pigment), and often progressive hearing loss due to abnormal ossicle/otic capsule collagen.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 6-year-old boy presents with a painless limp for several weeks and restricted hip abduction and internal rotation; X-ray shows flattening and increased density (sclerosis) of the femoral head with no history of trauma. This is most consistent with:
opts: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head)
why: SCFE classically occurs in obese adolescents with an externally rotated limb and knee-referred pain, a different age group
Correct — classic Perthes presentation in a school-age boy

Late/neglected DDH can also cause a painless limp in a walking child, but the X-ray shows a shallow dysplastic acetabulum with a displaced femoral head, not a flattened sclerotic head in a normal acetabulum
Septic arthritis presents acutely with fever and refusal to bear weight, not an insidious painless limp
exp: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis, typically in boys aged 4-8, presenting with an insidious painless limp and restricted internal rotation/abduction; radiographs progress through sclerosis, fragmentation, and reossification stages.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 12-year-old boy presents with a painful, progressively enlarging swelling of the mid-shaft femur for 3 months, associated with low-grade fever and raised ESR. X-ray shows a lamellated onion-skin periosteal reaction with an ill-defined permeative lesion in the diaphysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Osteosarcoma classically produces a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle at the metaphysis, not diaphyseal onion-skin
Correct, diaphyseal round-cell tumor with onion-skin reaction and systemic symptoms
Osteochondroma is a painless metaphyseal exostosis
Chondrosarcoma typically affects older adults with a popcorn calcification pattern
exp: Ewing sarcoma (t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 translocation) is the classic diaphyseal round-cell bone tumor of children and adolescents that mimics infection with fever and raised inflammatory markers - the onion-skin periosteal reaction is the key radiologic discriminator from osteosarcoma's sunburst pattern.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A female newborn is noted on routine examination to have asymmetric thigh folds and a palpable clunk when the examiner adducts the flexed hip while applying posterior pressure, with the clunk reproduced by abducting the hip while applying anterior pressure. What condition do these two maneuvers (respectively) test for?
opts: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis; Trendelenburg test
Developmental dysplasia of the hip; Barlow and Ortolani maneuvers
Septic arthritis of the hip; Kernig's sign
why: SCFE presents in obese, peri-pubertal adolescents, not neonates
Correct, Barlow (adduction plus posterior pressure) provokes a dislocatable hip, Ortolani (abduction plus anterior pressure) reduces it with a palpable clunk
Perthes disease presents later (4-8 years) with a limp
Septic arthritis presents with an acutely ill, febrile infant, not these provocative maneuvers
exp: DDH screening in the newborn period (Barlow/Ortolani) is time-sensitive - after about 3 months of age these maneuvers become less reliable as the hip stabilizes even if dysplastic, and ultrasound (Graf method) becomes the preferred imaging modality; risk factors include female sex, breech presentation, and family history.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 16-year-old with a tibial shaft fracture in a cast develops severe pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive toe stretch, and a tense, swollen leg. What is the most reliable early sign of the underlying condition?
opts: Pain on passive stretching of the muscles
why: Wrong — pulses are often preserved until very late since compartment pressure typically exceeds capillary, not arterial, pressure first; absence is a late, unreliable early sign.
Correct — pain on passive stretch is the earliest, most sensitive clinical sign, present before vascular signs appear.
Wrong — pallor is a late sign reflecting arterial compromise, not an early finding.
Wrong — paralysis reflects advanced nerve ischemia, occurring late, by which point the window for salvage may have passed.
exp: Compartment syndrome's classic 6 P's are pain, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia, pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive muscle stretch are the earliest and most sensitive signs; pulselessness and paralysis are late findings. Diagnosis is confirmed by compartment pressure measurement (delta pressure under 30 mmHg from diastolic indicates fasciotomy) — don't wait for pulselessness to act.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A child with a chronic discharging sinus over the tibia, 6 weeks after acute osteomyelitis, has an X-ray showing a dense necrotic bone fragment surrounded by new reactive bone. What are these two findings called respectively?
why: Wrong — this reverses the terms; the involucrum is the new bone sheath, not the necrotic fragment.
Correct — necrotic dead bone is the sequestrum, and the surrounding new reactive bone is the involucrum, correctly ordered.
Wrong — Brodie's abscess is a localized subacute intraosseous abscess, not this pair; the cloaca is the drainage opening, not the new bone.
Wrong — the cloaca is the sinus opening in the involucrum, not synonymous with the reactive bone itself.
exp: In chronic osteomyelitis, the sequestrum is the necrotic, avascular fragment of dead bone (radiodense, separated from viable bone), while the involucrum is the living, new reactive periosteal bone forming a sheath around it. Cloacae are openings in the involucrum through which pus and sequestra drain to a skin sinus. This chronic picture requires surgical debridement (sequestrectomy) in addition to antibiotics.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 70-year-old woman sustains a displaced subcapital femoral neck fracture after a fall. Which vessel is most critical to femoral head viability and is most often disrupted in this injury?
why: Wrong — the lateral femoral circumflex artery contributes less to femoral head supply than the medial one.
Wrong — the artery in the ligamentum teres (from the obturator artery) is a minor, inconsistent contributor, especially in adults.
Wrong — the superior gluteal artery supplies the gluteal muscles, not the femoral head.
Correct — the MFCA is the dominant blood supply to the femoral head via retinacular vessels, disrupted in displaced neck fractures, causing AVN.
exp: The medial femoral circumflex artery, a branch of the profunda femoris, supplies the majority of blood to the femoral head via retinacular vessels along the femoral neck. Displaced (Garden III/IV) subcapital fractures disrupt these vessels, causing high rates of avascular necrosis, which is why urgent reduction and fixation, or arthroplasty in the elderly, is favored over delayed management.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A patient with a fracture-dislocation at the elbow develops weakness of finger abduction and adduction, hypothenar wasting, and clawing of the ring and little fingers. Which nerve is injured?
why: Wrong — median nerve injury causes an ape thumb deformity and thenar wasting with sensory loss over the lateral 3.5 fingers, not ulnar-sided clawing.
Wrong — radial nerve injury classically causes wrist drop, not intrinsic hand muscle clawing.
Correct — claw hand affecting the ring and little fingers with hypothenar wasting and interossei weakness is classic ulnar nerve injury, common at the elbow.
Wrong — musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion (biceps/brachialis), unrelated to hand intrinsics or clawing.
exp: Ulnar nerve injury at the elbow (cubital tunnel compression, medial epicondyle fracture, or elbow dislocation) causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles (interossei), hypothenar wasting, and a claw hand deformity most marked in the ring and little fingers, since the ulnar-innervated lumbricals to these fingers are denervated while long flexor/extensor tendons act unopposed. Distal lesions paradoxically show a more pronounced claw (ulnar paradox) than proximal ones.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 3-year-old boy has progressive genu varum despite vitamin D3 supplementation given since infancy for presumed rickets. Investigations show normal serum calcium, low serum phosphate, normal serum bicarbonate, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Nutritional rickets responds to adequate vitamin D therapy — persistence of deformity despite supplementation argues against a simple dietary deficiency.
RTA type 1 also causes hypophosphatemic rachitic bone disease but is accompanied by a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (low serum bicarbonate), which is absent here.
Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcemia (often with hyperphosphatemia), not the normocalcemic hypophosphatemia seen in this child.

Correct — normal calcium, low phosphate, normal bicarbonate, and failure to respond to vitamin D point to FGF23-mediated renal phosphate wasting (X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, PHEX mutation), the most common inherited rickets.
exp: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (vitamin D-resistant rickets) is caused by excess FGF23 activity (classically PHEX gene mutations) causing renal phosphate wasting; unlike nutritional rickets it does NOT respond to standard vitamin D dosing — labs show normal calcium, low phosphate, and normal bicarbonate (distinguishing it from RTA), and treatment requires oral phosphate supplementation plus calcitriol.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 40-year-old man with chronic low back pain develops sudden bilateral leg weakness, saddle-area numbness, and new urinary retention with overflow incontinence after heavy lifting. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Outpatient MRI within one week and physiotherapy
Emergency MRI spine and surgical decompression within 48 hours
Epidural steroid injection for symptomatic relief
Bed rest with NSAIDs and reassessment in 2 weeks
why: Delaying imaging/treatment by a week risks permanent bladder and neurological damage
Correct — emergency imaging plus prompt surgical decompression is standard for cauda equina syndrome
Epidural steroids have no role in acute cauda equina syndrome and would dangerously delay definitive surgery
Conservative management is inappropriate and hazardous given the red-flag features present
exp: Bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, and new bladder dysfunction (retention with overflow) are red-flag features of cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency; urgent MRI followed by decompression done as early as feasible offers the best chance of neurological and bladder recovery.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressive pain and swelling around the knee for 2 months. X-ray of the distal femur shows a sunburst pattern of periosteal new bone formation and a Codman triangle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — metaphyseal sunburst pattern plus Codman triangle in an adolescent is textbook osteosarcoma
Ewing sarcoma is diaphyseal with an onion-skin lamellated periosteal reaction, typically in a slightly younger age group
Osteochondroma is a cartilage-capped exostosis without an aggressive periosteal reaction
Giant cell tumor is epiphyseal/subarticular in skeletally mature patients (20-40 years) with a soap-bubble lytic appearance
exp: Osteosarcoma is the classic bone tumor of adolescence, arising at the metaphysis of long bones (distal femur is the commonest site, followed by proximal tibia and proximal humerus), with sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle (elevated periosteum) as its hallmark radiographic signs. Contrast with Ewing sarcoma (diaphyseal, onion-skin reaction, slightly younger patients) and giant cell tumor (epiphyseal, soap-bubble lysis, skeletally mature patients).

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 13-year-old obese boy presents with a 3-week history of a limp and dull pain referred to the knee, worse on activity; the affected leg lies externally rotated at rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — obese adolescent boy, insidious limp, knee-referred pain, externally rotated limb is classic SCFE
Perthes disease typically affects a younger age group (4-8 years) and is not linked to obesity
Transient synovitis is acute (days, not weeks) and usually follows a viral illness in younger children
Septic arthritis presents acutely with fever, severe pain, and refusal to bear weight, not an indolent 3-week course
exp: SCFE classically affects obese adolescent boys (peak 12-14 years) with an insidious limp and knee pain referred via the obturator nerve, the limb externally rotated at rest with loss of internal rotation; it is confirmed when Klein's line fails to intersect the femoral head on AP hip X-ray.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 6-year-old girl sustains a supracondylar fracture of the humerus after falling on an outstretched hand. She cannot make an OK sign by pinching her thumb and index finger together, but sensation over the hand is normal. Injury to which nerve best explains this finding?
opts: Anterior interosseous nerve (branch of median nerve)
why: Ulnar nerve injury causes claw hand and sensory loss over the medial one-and-a-half fingers, not an isolated pinch-grip deficit.
Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop, not a failed OK sign.
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies biceps and brachialis, affecting elbow flexion, not pinch grip.
Correct - the AIN is a pure motor branch of the median nerve supplying flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger, so injury weakens pinch without sensory loss.
exp: The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), a pure motor branch of the median nerve, is the nerve most often injured in paediatric supracondylar humeral fractures. It supplies flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus (index), so injury produces an inability to make the OK sign (pulp-to-pulp pinch becomes flat-to-flat) with normal sensation, since AIN carries no cutaneous fibres.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 24-year-old man sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation during a fall while playing volleyball. After reduction he has weakness of abduction beyond 15 degrees and numbness over the regimental badge area of the lateral shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why: Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion/biceps with lateral forearm numbness, unrelated to shoulder dislocation.
Suprascapular nerve injury weakens supraspinatus/infraspinatus without this cutaneous loss.
Radial nerve injury follows mid-shaft humeral fracture with wrist drop, not shoulder dislocation.
Correct — classic axillary nerve injury pattern.
exp: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and is the nerve most vulnerable in anterior shoulder dislocation or surgical-neck fracture, producing deltoid weakness (loss of abduction beyond the first ~15 degrees) plus sensory loss over the regimental badge area.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman undergoes DEXA scanning of the lumbar spine, which reports a T-score of -2.7. How should her bone mineral density status be classified?
why: Normal requires a T-score of -1.0 or higher
Osteopenia is a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5, less severe than this reading
Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect diagnosed biochemically and histologically, not by DEXA T-score criteria
Correct — WHO criteria define osteoporosis as a T-score of -2.5 or lower, which -2.7 satisfies
exp: WHO DEXA classification: T-score of -1.0 or above is normal, -1.0 to -2.5 is osteopenia, -2.5 or below is osteoporosis, and osteoporosis with a fragility fracture is severe/established osteoporosis. A T-score of -2.7 is osteoporosis, not osteopenia.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 25-year-old man sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation. On examination after reduction, he has weakness of arm abduction beyond 15 degrees and numbness over the regimental badge area. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why: Correct — the axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and is most vulnerable to stretch injury in anterior shoulder dislocation
Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and numbs the lateral forearm, not this pattern
Suprascapular nerve injury weakens supraspinatus and infraspinatus (abduction initiation, external rotation) but causes no regimental-badge sensory loss
Radial nerve is classically injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures causing wrist drop, not typically in shoulder dislocation
exp: Anterior shoulder dislocation is the classic cause of axillary nerve injury: test deltoid function (abduction beyond about 15 degrees, once supraspinatus has initiated it) and sensation over the regimental badge area before and after any reduction attempt.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 68-year-old man presents with progressively increasing hat size, bowing of the tibia, and deep bone pain. Serum calcium and phosphate are normal, but serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
exp: Paget disease of bone causes disorganized excessive bone remodeling with markedly raised ALP but normal serum calcium and phosphate. This normocalcemic, normophosphatemic profile with a very high ALP is the key discriminator from osteomalacia and hyperparathyroidism. Watch for long-term risk of osteosarcoma and high-output cardiac failure.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: An 8-month-old exclusively breastfed infant presents with delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, bowing of the legs, and beading of the costochondral junctions (rachitic rosary). Serum calcium is low-normal, phosphate is low, and alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated. Which radiographic finding at the wrist would best support the diagnosis?
opts: Cupping and fraying of the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses
Subperiosteal bone resorption of the radial aspect of the middle phalanges
Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur
exp: In nutritional (vitamin D deficiency) rickets, the earliest and most specific radiographic changes occur at the rapidly growing metaphyses, cupping, fraying, and splaying, best seen at the distal radius/ulna and the costochondral junctions. Looser's zones are the analogous finding in adult osteomalacia, not childhood rickets, and are a common point of confusion.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 22-year-old man sustains a closed femoral shaft fracture in a road traffic accident. On day 2, he develops sudden breathlessness, confusion, and a petechial rash over the chest, neck, and axillae, with a PaO2 of 58 mmHg on room air. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute respiratory distress syndrome due to aspiration
why: Pulmonary embolism gives no petechial rash and usually comes later
Correct: hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae 24-72 hours after a long-bone fracture are fat embolism syndrome
Aspiration ARDS needs an aspiration event and gives no petechiae
Compartment syndrome causes local limb pain and tension, not a systemic triad
exp: Fat embolism syndrome classically follows long-bone (especially femoral shaft) or pelvic fractures within 24-72 hours, presenting as a triad of respiratory distress/hypoxemia, neurological changes (confusion, agitation), and a petechial rash over the chest, neck, axillae, and conjunctivae. Pulmonary thromboembolism lacks the petechial rash and usually presents later; ARDS from aspiration and compartment syndrome do not produce this systemic triad.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 30-year-old man sustains a mid-shaft humeral shaft fracture in a road traffic accident. On examination he is unable to extend his wrist and fingers, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the first web space. Which nerve is most likely injured?
exp: The radial nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove of the humeral shaft and is the nerve most commonly injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures, producing wrist drop and sensory loss over the first dorsal web space. Most are neurapraxias managed with splinting and observation for 3-4 months before considering exploration.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motorcycle collision with an unstable pelvic fracture. He has blood at the external urethral meatus and a boggy, high-riding prostate on digital rectal examination. What is the most appropriate next step before attempting bladder catheterization?
exp: Blood at the meatus with a high-riding, boggy prostate after pelvic fracture signals a posterior urethral injury. A retrograde urethrogram must be performed before any catheterization attempt, since blind instrumentation risks converting a partial urethral tear into a complete transection and introducing infection along the false tract.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 30-year-old man sustains a mid-shaft fracture of the humerus after a road traffic accident. On examination he is unable to extend his wrist and fingers, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the first web space. Which nerve is most likely injured?
exp: The radial nerve winds through the spiral groove of the humerus and is the nerve most vulnerable in mid-shaft humeral shaft fractures, producing wrist drop and sensory loss over the first dorsal web space; most such injuries are neurapraxias managed conservatively with a wrist-drop splint since spontaneous recovery occurs in the majority within 3-4 months.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 24-year-old man sustains a flexion-type axial loading injury to the thoracic spine in a road traffic accident. On examination, he has bilateral loss of motor power, pain, and temperature sensation below the level of injury, but proprioception and vibration sense in the lower limbs are preserved. Which spinal cord syndrome does this represent?
why: central cord syndrome follows hyperextension injury in an older patient with spondylosis, causing upper-limb-predominant weakness, not this pattern
bilateral motor plus spinothalamic loss with preserved dorsal column function after axial/flexion trauma is classic anterior cord syndrome
Brown-Sequard syndrome follows hemisection with contralateral pain/temperature loss, not bilateral symmetric loss
isolated posterior cord syndrome would spare motor and spinothalamic function, the opposite of this presentation
exp: Anterior cord syndrome results from injury to the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, typically from flexion-axial loading injuries or anterior spinal artery infarction, causing bilateral loss of motor function and spinothalamic sensation below the lesion while the dorsal columns are spared. It carries the worst prognosis for motor recovery among the incomplete cord syndromes.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Image described: X-ray of the proximal femur in a 14-year-old girl with irregular cafe-au-lait macules (coast of Maine borders) and precocious puberty shows a ground-glass lesion with a curved varus deformity of the proximal femur. What is the diagnosis?
why: osteofibrous dysplasia typically affects the tibial diaphysis in young children, not the proximal femur with this syndromic picture
unicameral bone cysts are lucent, not ground-glass, with a fallen-fragment sign, without endocrine/skin findings
non-ossifying fibroma is an eccentric cortical lucent lesion, unrelated to the syndromic triad
ground-glass lesion, shepherd's crook femur, irregular cafe-au-lait spots, and precocious puberty together confirm McCune-Albright fibrous dysplasia
exp: McCune-Albright syndrome is a mosaic GNAS gene disorder with the triad of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, irregular cafe-au-lait macules, and autonomous endocrine hyperfunction such as precocious puberty. The fibrous dysplasia lesions show a classic ground-glass matrix on X-ray, and proximal femur involvement causes progressive coxa vara producing the pathognomonic shepherd's crook deformity, predisposing to pathological fracture.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: Image described: hand X-ray of a 55-year-old woman with recurrent renal calculi and vague bone pain shows subperiosteal bone resorption along the radial aspect of the middle phalanges. Serum calcium is elevated and phosphate is low. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
opts: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease
why: secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD is associated with hypocalcaemia (or normal) and hyperphosphataemia, the opposite picture
hypercalcaemia plus hypophosphataemia plus subperiosteal resorption confirms primary hyperparathyroidism
osteomalacia shows Looser zones and a mineralization defect, not subperiosteal resorption
multiple myeloma causes punched-out lytic lesions and hypercalcaemia but not this specific resorption pattern
exp: Primary hyperparathyroidism, most often from a solitary parathyroid adenoma, causes hypercalcaemia with hypophosphataemia and classically produces subperiosteal bone resorption along the radial border of the middle phalanges, alongside renal calculi, bone pain, abdominal symptoms, and psychiatric changes. Diagnosis is confirmed by an elevated or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone level in the setting of hypercalcaemia.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 28-year-old man punches a wall and presents with pain and swelling at the base of his thumb. X-ray shows an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal, with a small ulnar fragment held in place by the anterior oblique ligament while the larger metacarpal shaft fragment is displaced proximally by the abductor pollicis longus. What is the diagnosis?
why: a Rolando fracture is a comminuted, three-part version of the same injury, not this simple two-part pattern
gamekeeper's thumb is an ulnar collateral ligament injury of the thumb MCP joint, not a metacarpal base fracture
the two-fragment pattern with the described ligamentous anatomy is the classic Bennett fracture
De Quervain's tenosynovitis is an overuse tendinopathy unrelated to trauma or fracture
exp: A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation at the base of the first metacarpal, where a small volar-ulnar fragment remains attached to the trapezium via the anterior oblique ligament while the larger metacarpal shaft fragment subluxates proximally and radially, pulled by the abductor pollicis longus. Because it is intra-articular and unstable, it usually requires reduction with internal fixation to prevent post-traumatic arthritis.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 45-year-old woman complains of burning pain and paraesthesiae over the sole of her foot, worse at night, for several months. Examination shows a positive Tinel's sign on percussion just posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus. Which nerve entrapment is responsible?
opts: Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck
Sural nerve at the lateral ankle
Deep peroneal nerve at the dorsum of the foot
Posterior tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel
why: common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular neck causes foot drop with dorsal foot/lateral leg sensory loss, not plantar burning pain
sural nerve entrapment causes lateral foot/ankle sensory symptoms, not sole-predominant burning pain
deep peroneal nerve entrapment causes symptoms over the first dorsal web space, not the sole
posterior tibial nerve entrapment in the tarsal tunnel matches the location of Tinel's sign and the plantar symptom distribution
exp: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is an entrapment neuropathy of the posterior tibial nerve as it passes beneath the flexor retinaculum posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus, causing burning pain and paraesthesiae over the sole of the foot, characteristically worse at night. A positive Tinel's sign over the tarsal tunnel supports the diagnosis; nerve conduction studies confirm it, and management ranges from orthoses to surgical release.

subject: Orthopaedics
q: A 12-year-old boy falls onto an outstretched hand while skating. Image described: wrist X-ray shows a fracture line running through the distal radial growth plate (physis) and extending into a triangular fragment of the metaphysis, with the epiphysis remaining anatomically aligned with the carpus. Which Salter-Harris type is this?
opts: Type II - fracture through physis and metaphysis
Type I - fracture confined to the physis only
Type III - fracture through physis and epiphysis
Type IV - fracture through metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis
why: correct: metaphyseal fragment plus a physeal fracture line define Salter-Harris Type II, the commonest paediatric physeal injury with generally good prognosis
Type I is a pure transphyseal separation with no metaphyseal or epiphyseal fragment, not matching the triangular metaphyseal piece described
Type III crosses into the epiphysis and articular surface, not described in this fracture pattern
Type IV crosses both metaphysis and epiphysis in one line, a different pattern from the isolated metaphyseal fragment described
exp: Salter-Harris type II is the commonest paediatric physeal injury (about 75 percent), classically producing a metaphyseal fragment (the Thurston-Holland sign) attached to the epiphysis while the fracture line runs along the physis; it generally has a good prognosis since the germinal reserve zone of the physis is spared. Type III and IV fractures cross into the epiphysis and carry a higher risk of growth arrest because they disrupt the articular surface and germinal layer.
